# curl & jq

curl is the universal command-line HTTP client. It's preinstalled on macOS, most Linux distributions and Windows 10/11 (as `curl.exe`). A curl command is the most portable bug-report artifact: anyone can run it, it shows exactly what was sent, and it fits in a ticket or a CI script. jq is its natural partner. It reads JSON from curl and extracts, filters or checks the fields you care about.

| Key fact | Details |
| --- | --- |
| **Install** | Usually preinstalled. jq: `brew install jq`, `sudo apt install jq`, `winget install jqlang.jq` |
| **Windows note** | In Windows PowerShell 5.1, `curl` is an alias for `Invoke-WebRequest`. Type `curl.exe` to get real curl |
| **Best for** | Minimal reproductions, smoke checks, timing and TLS diagnostics, CI scripts |
| **Practice API** | `https://postman-echo.com` echoes your request back as JSON |

```diagram
Copy as cURL from DevTools (or write from scratch) → strip noise headers → curl -i / -v to see status and headers → add body, auth and cookies → jq to read the JSON → -w timing and --fail for scripts → paste the final command into the bug report
```

## First requests: GET, status, headers and verbose mode

```bash
curl https://postman-echo.com/get?env=qa                 # body only
curl -i https://postman-echo.com/get?env=qa              # status line + headers + body
curl -I https://example.com                              # HEAD request: headers only
curl -v https://example.com                              # verbose: DNS, TLS, request and response headers
curl -L http://github.com                                # follow redirects (301/302)
curl -sS -o page.html https://example.com                # silent, but still show errors; save to a file
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://postman-echo.com/status/404
```

How to read `curl -v` output:

1. Lines starting with `*` are connection details: the IP address, TLS version, certificate and the negotiated HTTP version.
2. Lines starting with `>` are the request exactly as sent: method, path, `Host` and the other headers.
3. Lines starting with `<` are the response status and headers.
4. The body follows after the headers.

> **QA tip:** `-w "%{http_code}"` combined with `-o /dev/null` prints only the status code. That's the easiest way to check many URLs in a loop. On Windows use `-o NUL`.

## Sending data: JSON, forms and file uploads

```bash
# JSON, short form (curl 7.82+): sets Content-Type and Accept to application/json
curl --json '{"name":"QA","role":"tester"}' https://postman-echo.com/post

# JSON, explicit form that works with any curl version
curl -X POST https://postman-echo.com/post \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"QA","role":"tester"}'

# JSON from a file, handy for long payloads
curl --json @payload.json https://postman-echo.com/post

# Classic HTML form (application/x-www-form-urlencoded)
curl -d "email=qa@example.test" -d "password=secret" https://postman-echo.com/post

# File upload (multipart/form-data)
curl -F "file=@screenshot.png" -F "comment=layout bug" https://postman-echo.com/post

# Other methods
curl -X PUT    --json '{"status":"done"}' https://postman-echo.com/put
curl -X DELETE https://postman-echo.com/delete
```

Quoting differs between shells. In bash and zsh, wrap JSON in single quotes. In Windows `cmd.exe`, use double quotes outside and escape the inner ones (`"{\"name\":\"QA\"}"`), or simply keep the JSON in a file and send it with `@payload.json`.

> **Caveat:** `-d` without `-X` sends a POST. Adding `-X GET` to a command with `-d` sends a GET with a body, which many servers reject or ignore. Use `-G` if you want `-d` values in the query string instead.

## Auth headers, Basic auth and cookie jars

```bash
# Bearer token from an environment variable, so it stays out of shell history
export TOKEN="paste-test-token-here"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://postman-echo.com/headers

# Basic auth (Postman Echo accepts postman / password)
curl -u postman:password https://postman-echo.com/basic-auth

# API key in a header
curl -H "x-api-key: $API_KEY" https://api.example.test/v1/items

# Save cookies the server sets, then send them back on the next call
curl -c cookies.txt "https://postman-echo.com/cookies/set?session=abc123"
curl -b cookies.txt https://postman-echo.com/cookies
```

The cookie jar (`-c` to write, `-b` to read) lets you script a real session: log in once, then call the protected endpoints with the same cookies.

> **QA tip:** Negative auth checks are one-liners: drop the header (expect `401`), send a garbage token (expect `401`), or use a read-only user on a write endpoint (expect `403`).

## Timing and TLS diagnostics with -w, --resolve and timeouts

`-w` (`--write-out`) prints variables after the transfer. This breaks a slow request into its phases:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null https://example.com -w \
"dns:     %{time_namelookup}s
connect: %{time_connect}s
tls:     %{time_appconnect}s
ttfb:    %{time_starttransfer}s
total:   %{time_total}s
status:  %{http_code}  ip: %{remote_ip}  http: %{http_version}
"
```

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `time_namelookup` | DNS resolution finished |
| `time_connect` | TCP connection established |
| `time_appconnect` | TLS handshake finished (0 for plain HTTP) |
| `time_starttransfer` | First byte of the response arrived (TTFB) |
| `time_total` | Whole transfer finished |

All values are cumulative from the start. A big gap between `time_appconnect` and `time_starttransfer` means the server is thinking, not the network.

```bash
# Hit a specific server behind a load balancer or before DNS is switched
curl --resolve api.example.test:443:10.0.0.5 https://api.example.test/health

# Fail fast instead of hanging
curl --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 https://api.example.test/slow

# Force a protocol version
curl --http1.1 https://example.com
curl --http2 https://example.com

# Show certificate details
curl -v https://example.com 2>&1 | grep -E "subject:|issuer:|expire date:"
```

> **Caveat:** `-k` / `--insecure` skips certificate checks. It's acceptable on a throwaway local environment, but never "fix" a certificate bug with it. The certificate error is often the bug.

## Reading JSON with jq

```bash
# Pretty-print
curl -s https://postman-echo.com/get?env=qa | jq .

# One field, raw string without quotes
curl -s https://postman-echo.com/get?env=qa | jq -r '.args.env'

# Field with a dash in the name
curl -s https://postman-echo.com/headers | jq -r '.headers["user-agent"]'

# Count items, pick fields, filter
jq '.items | length' response.json
jq '.items[] | {id, status}' response.json
jq '.items[] | select(.status == "failed") | .id' response.json

# Use jq as an assertion: exit code 1 if the expression is false or null
curl -s https://postman-echo.com/get?env=qa | jq -e '.args.env == "qa"' > /dev/null && echo PASS
```

| jq filter | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `.` | Whole document, pretty-printed |
| `.user.email` | Nested field |
| `.items[0]` | First array element |
| `.items[]` | Each element in turn |
| `select(.price > 100)` | Keep only matching elements |
| `map(.id)` | Array of one field |
| `keys` | Field names of an object |
| `-r` | Raw output (no quotes) |
| `-e` | Exit code reflects the result, useful in scripts |

## curl in scripts and CI: --fail, retries and exit codes

By default curl exits with code `0` even when the server returns `404` or `500`, because the HTTP transfer itself worked. In scripts, ask curl to treat HTTP errors as failures:

```bash
# Exit code 22 on HTTP >= 400, and still print the error body
curl --fail-with-body -sS https://postman-echo.com/status/500

# Retry transient failures (connection errors, 408, 429, 5xx) 3 times, 2 s apart
curl --fail --retry 3 --retry-delay 2 -sS https://api.example.test/health

# Smoke check used in a pipeline
status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "$BASE_URL/health")
[ "$status" = "200" ] || { echo "Health check failed: $status"; exit 1; }
```

**From browser to terminal:** in Chrome DevTools, right-click a request → **Copy** → **Copy as cURL**. Then delete headers that don't matter for the bug (`sec-ch-ua`, `accept-language`, tracking cookies). Keep the minimum that still reproduces the failure.

![Chrome DevTools copy options for requests, including cURL](https://developer.chrome.com/static/docs/devtools/network/reference/image/copy-all-options.png "Official Chrome DevTools documentation screenshot: copy options for all requests, including Copy all as cURL.")

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Show status and headers | `curl -i URL` |
| Debug connection and TLS | `curl -v URL` |
| Follow redirects | `curl -L URL` |
| POST JSON | `curl --json '{"a":1}' URL` |
| Upload a file | `curl -F "file=@a.png" URL` |
| Bearer token | `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" URL` |
| Basic auth | `curl -u user:pass URL` |
| Cookie session | `-c jar.txt` then `-b jar.txt` |
| Only the status code | `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" URL` |
| Timing breakdown | `-w "%{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}"` |
| Pin DNS to one server | `--resolve host:443:10.0.0.5` |
| Fail the script on HTTP errors | `--fail-with-body` |
| Extract a JSON field | `curl -s URL` piped into `jq -r '.field'` |

## Summary

- `-i` and `-v` show exactly what went over the wire. Use them before guessing.
- `--json`, `-d` and `-F` cover JSON, forms and uploads. `-H`, `-u` and the cookie jar cover authentication.
- `-w` timing variables separate DNS, connect, TLS, server time and download. `--resolve` and timeouts help with environment and network issues.
- jq turns curl into a test: extract fields with `-r` and assert with `-e`. In CI, always use `--fail-with-body` so HTTP errors fail the job.
